{"id": "53:47/q01", "question": "How does wa anna connect this clause to its context?", "turns_on": "Whether the opening is read wa anna as a continued clause or wa inna as a fresh assertion.", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q01/p1", "position": "It continues the series of truths conveyed in the scriptures of Moses and Abraham.", "reasons": "Study Quran says all verses 42–50 except 46 begin wa anna and continue the account of those scriptures in 36–41."}, {"id": "53:47/q01/p2", "position": "Read as wa inna, it opens an independent emphatic statement: truly or surely.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this alternative vocalization for the repeated clauses."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q02", "question": "What does 'upon Him' signify here?", "turns_on": "Whether ʿalā denotes rational obligation, God's self-binding promise, assignment to His power, or emphasis directed at deniers.", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q02/p1", "position": "Resurrection is assured by God's own promise and wisdom, without an obligation imposed on Him.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi says promised reward and compensation for earthly suffering require a further life of judgment and justice. Al-Razi cites God's promise in 36:12. Al-Baydawi, al-Biqai, Bursawi, al-Alusi, Ibn Ashur, and Tabatabai stress fulfillment of a promise or irrevocable decree; al-Biqai says God does not change His word, Ibn Ashur likens the wording to an assured right and cites 6:12, and Tabatabai says He has said He will not break His promise. Bursawi also says wisdom calls for bodily recompense and believers' gradual perfection: this world cannot contain one person's full reward, demanding immediate results is discourteous, and a purified divine gift should be accepted with trust in God's choice."}, {"id": "53:47/q02/p2", "position": "Reason or divine wisdom makes resurrection incumbent on God so that good and evil receive their due.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi invokes the force of ʿalā and says resurrection is owed to those due reward or compensation, against the claim that nothing is incumbent on God. Al-Kashshaf and al-Zamakhshari as reported by al-Razi and al-Alusi ground obligation in wise requital; al-Alusi questions that Muʿtazilite approach."}, {"id": "53:47/q02/p3", "position": "Resurrection rests with God as the one able and assigned to bring it about.", "reasons": "Al-Razi offers this as an alternative to rational obligation; Asad renders the phrase literally as the second coming to life resting upon God."}, {"id": "53:47/q02/p4", "position": "The emphatic 'upon Him' addresses deniers, making resurrection sound as if God has imposed it upon Himself.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this explanation from Abu Hayyan's al-Bahr."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q03", "question": "What does al-nashʾa mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q03/p1", "position": "A newly brought into being, fashioned creation.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi calls it newly made creation and distinguishes initial life from resurrection. Al-Tabrisi says it is fashioned origination, as distinct from merely willing something. Al-Razi derives both noun forms from intransitive nashaʾa."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q04", "question": "How is al-nashʾa read and formed?", "turns_on": "The presence or absence of an alif after shīn, with corresponding verbal-noun patterns.", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q04/p1", "position": "The short nashʾa, without an alif after shīn, is read.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya calls this the common reading, with still shīn and hamza. Ibn al-Jazari says the remaining readers omit the alif here and in al-ʿAnkabut and al-Waqiʿa; al-Biqaʿi also contrasts them with the lengtheners. Al-Razi analyzes it as a faʿla verbal noun for one occurrence. Qiraat-ER calls both forms canonical."}, {"id": "53:47/q04/p2", "position": "The long nashāʾa, with an alif after shīn, is read.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf records the form; Ibn Atiyya attributes it to Abu ʿAmr and al-Aʿraj, while al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, Ibn al-Jazari, al-Biqaʿi and al-Alusi attribute it to Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr. Ibn al-Jazari gives the same distribution in al-ʿAnkabut and al-Waqiʿa. Al-Razi calls it a faʿāla verbal noun; al-Baydawi and al-Alusi also say it is a Form I nashaʾa verbal noun. Al-Qurtubi associates the reading with promised resurrection; Qiraat-ER calls both forms canonical and suggests the long form may stress an extended rather than punctual process."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q05", "question": "Why say al-nashʾa rather than al-inshāʾ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q05/p1", "position": "It asserts that the new creation actually comes to exist.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says al-inshāʾ would be the expected noun for causing to arise, but it could denote an attempt with no result, whereas al-nashʾa confirms the result."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q06", "question": "What does calling it 'the other creation' add?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q06/p1", "position": "It identifies a second creation already known and due from God, rather than merely saying creation happens once more.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says 'once more' need not presuppose a known first creation, whereas 'the other creation' points to the known second one."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q07", "question": "What is the other creation?", "turns_on": "Whether the nearby creation and provision sequence indicates fetal ensoulment or the destination and recompense context indicates resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q07/p1", "position": "The resurrection or recreation of people after death for the afterlife.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Abu Ubayda, Ibn Qutayba, al-Thaʿlabi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Nasafi and others identify raising after death. Al-Nahhas speaks of recreating the pair; Ibn Atiyya specifies restoration of bodies after decay in soil; al-Qurtubi specifies spirits returned to bodies. Al-Jishumi contrasts initial life and resurrection. Al-Tabrisi, al-Kashshaf, al-Baydawi, Tabatabai and Elmalili connect it with reward, punishment or compensation. Al-Razi reports this as most exegetes' view and notes contextual support from the final destination and full recompense (53:42, 53:41) and the use of the phrase in 29:20, while answering that this passage has just described creation from a drop. Ibn Kathir and Islahi argue that the first creation establishes God's ability to recreate; al-Biqaʿi says the first proves the second and God's promise ensures it. Islahi adds that justice and mercy fully appear in resurrection; Bursevi adds that wisdom gives believers their fitting perfection. Qurtubi's reading note calls it promised resurrection; Asad calls it the second coming to life, and al-Alusi and Kuranyolu give the usual afterlife explanation."}, {"id": "53:47/q07/p2", "position": "The ensoulment of the embryo, joining a noble human spirit to the body.", "reasons": "Al-Razi proposes this as an honor giving humans angel-like perception and cites 23:14: after sperm develops into bones, ensoulment makes humans distinct from animals and is called another creation. He argues that this passage has just recalled creation from a drop, and its sequence then moves from male and female to the human spirit and to provision in 53:48: mother's milk and father's support in childhood, earning in adulthood. Kuranyolu reports his suggestion and its preceding creation context."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q08", "question": "Must creatures perish before the second creation?", "turns_on": "Whether a second creation requires the first substances to cease existing.", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q08/p1", "position": "Yes; the second creation entails prior annihilation and restoration.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi reasons that what persists can cease only through an opposite or something functioning like one, so God annihilates then restores creation."}, {"id": "53:47/q08/p2", "position": "No; substances do not perish once they have come into existence.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi reports this as the view of some."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q09", "question": "How do substances come to cease?", "turns_on": "Whether cessation is direct annihilation, loss of renewed persistence, or cessation of a sustaining state.", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q09/p1", "position": "God directly annihilates them.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi reports Abu al-Husayn al-Khayyat's account."}, {"id": "53:47/q09/p2", "position": "God stops creating persistence in them.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi reports Abu al-Qasim's account."}, {"id": "53:47/q09/p3", "position": "God creates imperishable states in them, and they cease when those states cease.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi reports this as another position."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q10", "question": "How are perished substances restored?", "turns_on": "Whether restoration needs a distinct causal meaning beyond God's creating the substance again.", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q10/p1", "position": "God creates them again without a separate cause called restoration.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi holds this and objects that positing an additional restoring meaning produces an infinite regress of meanings."}, {"id": "53:47/q10/p2", "position": "An original existent comes to be by an agent, while a restored existent returns through a distinct cause called restoration.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi reports this view from some and argues that it entails an infinite regress of meanings."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q11", "question": "What inward resurrection parallels bodily resurrection?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q11/p1", "position": "Spiritual resurrection is a second birth into enduring divine attributes and heavenly realities after spiritual annihilation.", "reasons": "Bursawi compares bodily resurrection after full bodily annihilation and readiness for spirit with shedding human traits and readiness for divine effusion. Both births require a sound constitution: a malformed embryo miscarries and a malformed womb cannot conceive. He cites Jesus saying no one enters heaven's kingdom without being born twice, explaining the second bi

{"id": "53:47/q12", "question": "Why is there no emphatic huwa in this clause?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q12/p1", "position": "No rival could plausibly claim responsibility for resurrection, so the separator pronoun is unnecessary.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan extends this to creating the pair and destroying ʿAd. Al-Suhayli, as reported in al-Itqan, says huwa appears where a quality was claimed for someone besides God, such as making people laugh and weep (53:43), and is absent where no rival claim existed (including 53:45, 53:47, 53:50)."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q13", "question": "How does this clause follow the creation account and lead to what follows?", "turns_on": "Whether the surrounding human creation and provision sequence points forward to resurrection or continues with ensoulment.", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q13/p1", "position": "Human reproduction prepares an argument for resurrection, which the preceding account of life's beginning makes timely.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says reproduction, though known to the audience, independently proves resurrection, as in 21:104; that independent force explains the conjunction before this clause. Islahi says creation from a drop shows God can recreate, and Elmalili says paired creation in this world points to an afterlife."}, {"id": "53:47/q13/p2", "position": "The sequence proceeds from sexual creation to ensoulment and then to worldly provision in the next verse.", "reasons": "Al-Razi describes care through mother's milk and father's provision in childhood and earning in adulthood, matching 53:48."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q14", "question": "Which earlier scriptural words does this resurrection claim recall?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q14/p1", "position": "It echoes Abraham's declaration that God will bring him back after death in 26:81.", "reasons": "Islahi says the divine acts in this section echo Abraham's declaration of acquittal against his people in 26:78–82, with slight variations; the resurrection claim corresponds to 26:81."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q15", "question": "How does this verse fit the sūra's appeal to Moses' and Abraham's scriptures?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q15/p1", "position": "The section moves from reflection on human creation to enduring truths in those scriptures, with this clause in the continuing series.", "reasons": "Study Quran calls this the third section, says it turns to perennial truths attested in Moses' and Abraham's scriptures, and links the wa anna clauses of 42–50 to the scriptural discussion in 36–41."}, {"id": "53:47/q15/p2", "position": "Ancestry from Abraham and Moses does not entitle people to Paradise; their teaching and sacrifices are the point of the appeal.", "reasons": "Islahi condemns reliance on descent from those prophets and redirects attention to their teaching and sacrifices."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q16", "question": "What does this assertion teach about God's power and governance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q16/p1", "position": "The creator of the first life has power to recreate people after death.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir argues from initial creation to return on Judgment Day; al-Biqaʿi says the first creation proves the second, and Islahi makes the same argument from each person's creation from a drop while adding that resurrection permits divine justice and mercy to appear fully."}, {"id": "53:47/q16/p2", "position": "All events of life, death and the universe depend on God's will and power.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu reads verses 43–49 as examples of this comprehensive dependence."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q17", "question": "What ruling about an unconscious pilgrim is noted with this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q17/p1", "position": "Companions may perform the rites when customary conduct supplies the pilgrim's consent.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi treats customary consent as though the pilgrim had spoken."}]}
{"id": "53:47/q18", "question": "What example illustrates that word order can add meaning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "53:47/q18/p1", "position": "Different arrangements of the same comparison can make its likeness more emphatic.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani says two Zayd-and-lion similes share the basic comparison, but kaʾanna Zaydan al-asad makes Zayd's bravery virtually indistinguishable from a lion's through its word order and combination."}]}
{"id": "54:17/q01", "question": "How is the word ٱلْقُرْءَانَ read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "54:17/q01/p1", "position": "The hamza may be eased or dropped, yielding qurāna.", "reasons": "QIRAAT-ER attributes this hmz form to tashīl and the Hijazi tendency to lighten or elide hamza."}]}
{"id": "54:17/q02", "question": "What does God's making the Qur'an easy involve?", "turns_on": "Whether ease is located chiefly in recitation, memorization, comprehensible admonition, or preparation for the Qur'an's teaching purpose; some sources join these benefits. Al-Alusi favors admonition from context, while al-Islahi rejects restricting it to memorization or elementary Arabic comprehension.", "positions": [{"id": "54:17/q02/p1", "position": "God enabled human tongues to recite and speak the Qur'an, which otherwise they could not bear to utter.", "reasons": "Mujahid glosses ease as recitation in MUJAHID, IBNKATHIR, DURR and ALUSI; al-Suddi specifies tongues. Muqatil, al-Farra, Ibn Qutayba, Tustari and reports from Ibn Abbas, Anas and Hasan say creatures could not speak God's speech without divine easing; Muqatil adds recitation in every circumstance, Ibn Qutayba also listening. Al-Mawardi calls accessibility to speakers of every language miraculous. Ibn Kathir includes revelation in seven ahruf. Al-Alusi says the Anas report, even if authentic, need not interpret this verse and favors admonition in context."}, {"id": "54:17/q02/p2", "position": "God made the Qur'an easy to memorize completely and retain by heart.", "reasons": "Al-Farra and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, cited by many sources, contrast other revealed books: none is recited entirely from memory as the Qur'an is. Al-Zajjaj notes Torah and Gospel readers generally look at a written copy. Al-Qurtubi reports that Israelites, except Moses, Aaron, Joshua and Ezra, read Torah from a copy and marveled when Ezra rewrote it after a fire. Al-Qurtubi says God helps seekers and makes preservation nearly innate. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan cite its arrangement, sound or pleasant wording, lack of filler, and noble true meanings that engage hearts; al-Baydawi cites concision and pleasing wording, al-Alusi adds eloquence and lack of obscurity. Al-Islahi accepts memorization as a correct inference but rejects limiting taysir to it."}, {"id": "54:17/q02/p3", "position": "God made the Qur'an clear and understandable so people can reflect, learn, take warning and follow its guidance.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd glosses yassarna as 'made clear'; al-Tabari and al-Nahhas stress explanation and detail. Muqatil in al-Mawardi says its knowledge and derivation of meaning are eased. Al-Wahidi cites intelligible Arabic and 26:195; al-Tabrisi cites clear expression, proofs, sound rulings and true meanings, and explains that recalling proofs opens knowledge. Al-Zamakhshari in BURHAN describes interwoven admonition, promise and threat. Al-Biqai says Arabic familiar to its hearers, examples, eloquence, and stories make warning accessible; unsurpassed eloquence together with clarity is miraculous, and difficult matters reward elevated scholars (58:11). Ibn Kathir cites 38:29 and 19:97. Ibn Ashur sees guidance for varying capacities and a rebuke to those who turn away, linked to the preservation promise in 15:9. Al-Islahi specifies Quraysh Arabic, gradual revelation (17:106), early short teachings then elaboration (11:1), varied presentations (7:58), and complementary sura groups and pairs (39:23; 15:87). He rejects the claim that rudimentary Arabic automatically yields full understanding. Al-Tabatabai says simple and deep readers each grasp according to capacity."}, {"id": "54:17/q02/p4", "position": "God fitted or prepared the Qur'an for the work of remembrance, as one equips a mount or a person for a task.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi cite preparing or bridling a camel or horse; al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and al-Samin cite poetry using mayssiran for a bridled horse. Al-Islahi says taysir means fitting and equipping for a purpose; his cited poem by Mudarris ibn Rub'i describes equipping a leader for a campaign. He broadens this to the Qur'an's full means of educating Quraysh."}, {"id": "54:17/q02/p5", "position": "The ease includes recitation on the tongue and memorization, understanding and knowledge in different hearts.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri says different groups share these gifts and are all Qur'an people and God's elect; al-Biqai repeats him. The Study Quran calls this mercy to tongue, mind and heart. Ibn Kathir joins accessible wording and meaning; al-Biqai also includes honor for those who attend to it. Al-Islahi's early concise verses aided memorization, understanding, practice and transmission."}, {"id": "54:17/q02/p6", "position": "Yassarnā means simply 'We made easy' or 'facilitated'.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj supplies the direct gloss; Mujahid in al-Tabari and al-Nahhas says 'made manageable/easy'; al-Damghani gives yusr and taysir as facilitation, also used for an easy outcome in provision. Al-Elmalili says it may mean readily granted for reflection."}]}

Al-Wahidi distinguishes the recitation interpretation from reflection."}, {"id": "54:17/q03/p3", "position": "It means a broad work of educating and awakening knowledge already latent in people.", "reasons": "Al-Islahi says it includes educating, instructing, informing, warning, counseling and conclusively establishing truth; the Qur'an revives neglected innate treasures rather than importing alien knowledge. Al-Wasiti says the remembering heart is taught by the Qur'an's spirit. Al-Biqai describes recollection of former knowledge that one cannot independently summon."}]}
{"id": "54:17/q04", "question": "How does the lām in لِلذِّكْرِ work?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "54:17/q04/p1", "position": "It marks remembrance as the beneficiary of God's making easy, with a relation like transitivity.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur attaches the lām to yassarnā as a non-fixed adverbial, not an ordinary purpose object. He prefers Ibn Malik's label ma'na al-ta'diya over Ibn Hisham's shibh al-tamlik: its noun resembles the first object of 'clothe' or 'give'. He compares 42:11, 19:5, 36:72, 87:8 and 92:7,10; here remembrance is personified as a beneficiary of guidance, and yassarnā furnishes the metaphor's image. He says the lām's basic causal meaning developed into several conventional uses."}]}
{"id": "54:17/q05", "question": "What is the form and derivation of مُّدَّكِرٍ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "54:17/q05/p1", "position": "It is an iftiʿāl form from dhikr; consonants change and assimilate to produce doubled dāl.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi gives an original mudhtakir with tāʾ changing to dāl before assimilation; al-Wahidi reports Abu Ishaq's explanation that voiced dāl better suits dhāl than voiceless tāʾ and compares muzdajir. Ibn Atiyya describes tāʾ becoming dhāl then assimilation; Bursevi describes dhāl assimilating into tāʾ and becoming doubled dāl. Elmalili gives an underlying muztakir and Ibn Ashur a form mudhtadhkir, explaining the close articulation points. Al-Wahidi notes frequent dāl forms iddakar and muddakir, comparing taqwā, taqiya and taqāt. Abu Ali cites Sibawayh for a dhāl form in al-dhikr, supported by Ibn Muqbil's verse."}]}
{"id": "54:17/q06", "question": "Which readings are reported for مُّدَّكِرٍ?", "turns_on": "Whether the consonant is the standard doubled dāl or the reported dhāl form; Abu Hatim objects to the latter's assimilation rule.", "positions": [{"id": "54:17/q06/p1", "position": "The dāl form muddakir is the transmitted prophetic and common reading.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reports Abu Hatim's sound chain from the Prophet. Bursevi reports Ibn Mas'ud being corrected from a dhāl form to dāl; al-Durr gives Ibn Mas'ud's dhāl recitation beside the Prophet's dāl recitation. Ibn Ashur says this verse's reading is specifically transmitted from the Prophet and points to 12:45."}, {"id": "54:17/q06/p2", "position": "A dhāl form mudhakkir or muthakkir is reported from Ibn Mas'ud and Qatada.", "reasons": "Al-Durr says Ibn Mas'ud recited with dhāl while the Prophet recited with dāl; Bursevi says the Prophet corrected Ibn Mas'ud. Abu Hatim in Ibn Atiyya calls Qatada's dhāl assimilation poor because its proposed rule would change other words too."}]}
{"id": "54:17/q07", "question": "Whom does فَهَلْ مِن مُّدَّكِرٍ call for, and to do what?", "turns_on": "Whether the invitation centers on taking warning, seeking knowledge or good, reciting and retaining scripture, leaving sin, or recovering inward remembrance.", "positions": [{"id": "54:17/q07/p1", "position": "Someone who remembers, reflects and takes admonition from the Qur'an and its warning.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba and many commentators treat it as a summons to take heed; Muqatil in al-Wahidi specifies recognizing the warning's truth and fearing it. Al-Wahidi distinguishes the reflection reading from the recitation reading. Ibn Zayd in Abu Hayyan glosses muddakir as one taking admonition; Ibn Abbas in al-Durr says 'anyone who will remember'. Al-Tabrisi urges considering the Qur'an; al-Biqai says the question asks people to recall what God made accessible. Al-Qashani invokes the single way of truth and shared foundations of prophetic laws. KURANYOLU includes taking a lesson or instruction; Study Quran links it to 54:15."}, {"id": "54:17/q07/p2", "position": "A seeker of knowledge who will receive divine help to learn.", "reasons": "Matar al-Warraq's explanation appears in al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi, al-Jishumi, Ibn Kathir, al-Biqai and al-Durr; Ibn Kathir notes transmission by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir and al-Bukhari's definite suspended attribution. Qatada joins Matar in al-Jishumi and is also named by Ibn Kathir. Ibn Atiyya attributes a similar explanation to Mutarrif. Al-Nahhas says this is close to the first interpretation, whose apparent sense he favors. Al-Tabrisi says an eased path to knowledge gives strong reason to pursue learning."}, {"id": "54:17/q07/p3", "position": "A seeker of good who will be helped toward it.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas reports 'good or knowledge' and favors the first apparent interpretation while calling this close. Abu Bakr al-Warraq and Ibn Shawdhab in al-Qurtubi join good and knowledge; Abu Hayyan and al-Durr attribute the good-seeker gloss to Qatada, and KURANYOLU reports it from Tabari."}, {"id": "54:17/q07/p4", "position": "Someone who will recite, memorize, study and learn the Qur'an with God's help.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi spells out recitation, study, learning and understanding on the recitation interpretation. Ibn Atiyya says memorization keeps guidance and knowledge present; al-Qurtubi says God helps those seeking to memorize but elsewhere glosses the question simply as reciting. Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi give the memorization and divine-help reading; Ibn al-Jawzi urges recitation."}, {"id": "54:17/q07/p5", "position": "Someone who will be deterred from sin and abandon it.", "reasons": "Muhammad ibn Ka'b gives this gloss in Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir and al-Durr. Bursevi says a mindful person learns from the sign, fears God and leaves sin."}, {"id": "54:17/q07/p6", "position": "Someone who recalls the pretemporal covenant with God.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri reports a Sufi saying that God communicated through the Qur'an with some spirits before embodiment. Study Quran says either remembrance or admonition can evoke the pact of 7:172."}, {"id": "54:17/q07/p7", "position": "Someone whose heart has been taught by the Qur'an's spirit and recalls what God already brought to them.", "reasons": "Al-Wasiti, as reported by al-Sulami, ties the capacity to remember to inward teaching of the heart."}]}
{"id": "54:17/q08", "question": "What is the force of the closing question?", "turns_on": "Whether hal mainly invites a willing hearer or rebukes an audience that has failed to take heed.", "positions": [{"id": "54:17/q08/p1", "position": "It is an urgent call inviting listeners to remember and take heed.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi, al-Baghawi and al-Tabrisi treat the question as an exhortation.
